title: Sampling, quantization, and aliasing
summary: Explain sampling and quantization in plain words; turn a sampling rate into the time between samples and a sample count; count levels from bits; find the Nyquist frequency and the fake (alias) frequency a too-high tone turns into.
sourceNote: sampling_quantization.pdf, aliasing.pdf, Rosen & Howell (1991) ch. 14, Lab 2. Rewritten in plain steps: one idea per card.

sections.heading: Why a computer can't just store a wave

blocks.md: **You are on step 2 of the map:** the computer has to measure the sound and store it as numbers.
blocks.label: why

blocks.md: A real sound wave is smooth: it has a value at **every** instant, and each value can be any number. A computer can only store a **list** of numbers, each with limited precision. So we make two compromises:

blocks.body: Measuring the wave at regular moments in time, instead of at every instant. Like a movie: 24 still photos per second instead of continuous motion.
Rounding each measurement to one of a fixed set of allowed values. Like a ruler that only has marks every millimeter.

blocks.prompt: Which compromise is about WHEN we measure, and which is about HOW PRECISELY?
blocks.answer: Sampling is when (moments in time). Quantization is how precisely (allowed values).

sections.heading: Sampling: measuring many times a second

blocks.body: How many measurements per second, in Hz. Fₛ = 16,000 Hz means 16,000 numbers stored for every second of sound. (The little s stands for 'sampling'.)
The time between two measurements. It's the flip of the rate: **Tₛ = 1 / Fₛ**.

blocks.title: Rate ↔ interval, and counting samples
blocks.body:
Fₛ = 100 Hz  →  Tₛ = 1/100 = 0.01 s between samples
Fₛ = 16,000 Hz  →  Tₛ = 1/16,000 = 0.0000625 s

How many samples in a recording?
  samples = seconds × Fₛ
  4 s at 100 Hz  →  4 × 100 = 400 samples
  2.5 s at 16,000 Hz  →  40,000 samples

blocks.title: Sampling the same wave slowly and quickly

frames.caption: A real sound has a value at EVERY instant. A computer can't store infinitely many numbers, so it takes a measurement every so often.
Measure a 5 Hz wave 10 times per second (Fₛ = 10 Hz): only 2 measurements per repeat. The numbers jump 1, −1, 1, −1. You can barely tell it was a smooth wave.
Measure the same wave 50 times per second (Fₛ = 50 Hz): 10 measurements per repeat. Now the numbers clearly trace the smooth shape.
Each stored number is called a sample. x[0] is the first, x[1] the second, and so on. x[n] means 'sample number n'.

blocks.title: The formula for a sampled wave
blocks.body:
Sample number n is taken at time t = n / Fₛ.
So just replace t with n/Fₛ:

  x(t)  = A · cos(2π · F · t + ϕ)
  x[n]  = A · cos(2π · F · n/Fₛ + ϕ)

Nothing else changes. (Lab 3 Q4)

Lab 2 Q9: to get a better copy of the wave you need a **higher Fₛ** (same thing as a **shorter Tₛ**). Recording for longer does NOT make each part more accurate; it just gives you more of the same quality.

blocks.prompt: A recording at Fₛ = 8,000 Hz lasts 3 seconds. How many samples?

blocks.md: **Real numbers you'll see:** 44,100 Hz (music CDs), 48,000 Hz (video), 16,000 Hz (speech technology, including most speech recognizers), 8,000 Hz (phone calls).

blocks.body: Each sample is stored with a fixed number of **bits**. With b bits you get **2ᵇ allowed levels**. 3 bits → 2³ = 8 levels. 16 bits → 65,536 levels (CD quality).

blocks.md: Each measurement gets **snapped to a level**. In Koo's convention it snaps **down**: take the highest level that is not above the value. The small difference between the real value and the stored one is called **quantization error** (it sounds like faint noise). More bits = smaller steps = less error.

The smooth wave (green) can take any value; the stored signal (blue staircase) must sit on one of 2³ = 8 levels, snapping down to the highest level that doesn't exceed each sample. The red gap is quantization error: the noise that more bits shrink. At CD quality (16 bits) there are 65,536 levels, so the staircase hugs the wave far too closely to hear. Hover any part.

sections.heading: Aliasing: when a high sound pretends to be a low one

blocks.md: **Picture it.** In old movies, car wheels sometimes look like they spin backward. The camera only takes 24 pictures a second. If a spoke moves almost a full turn between pictures, it *looks* like it moved a little backward. Sampling sound too slowly does the same thing: a high frequency comes out looking like a lower one.

blocks.body: A fake frequency. After sampling, a too-high tone gives **exactly the same list of numbers** as some lower tone, so the computer can't tell them apart. The lower one is its alias.

The samples land exactly where a slow 1 Hz cosine (red, dashed) would put them: cos(2π·7·n/8) = cos(2π·1·n/8) for every n. The computer keeps only the dots, so it reconstructs the red wave, not the green one: the wagon wheel spinning backward, in audio. Hover any part.
blocks.slide: Two waves, one set of samples

blocks.body: Half the sampling rate: **Fₛ / 2**. It's the highest frequency you can store honestly. Anything above it turns into an alias.

blocks.title: Nyquist in three examples
blocks.body:
Fₛ = 16,000 Hz  →  Nyquist = 8,000 Hz
Fₛ = 8,000 Hz (phone)  →  Nyquist = 4,000 Hz
Fₛ = 44,100 Hz (CD)  →  Nyquist = 22,050 Hz

Flip it: to record up to F Hz, you need Fₛ of at least 2 × F.

blocks.title: Finding the fake frequency (the folding rule)

frames.caption: Step 1: find the Nyquist frequency, half the sampling rate. Anything above it will fake being something lower.
Step 2: is the tone above Nyquist? Yes, so it can't be stored honestly.
Step 3: when the tone is between Nyquist and Fₛ, the fake frequency is Fₛ minus the tone. It 'folds back' like a mirror around 5,000.
Check it as a mirror: the fake is as far below Nyquist as the real tone was above it.

lines: tone above Fₛ? subtract Fₛ first
frames.caption: Step 0 if the tone is even higher than Fₛ: subtract Fₛ until you're below Fₛ, then do the mirror step if it's still above Nyquist.

blocks.caption: Drag F past Fₛ/2 and watch the dashed alias appear through the same dots; the buttons play the true tone and the tone the computer keeps. Turn on quantization and drop to 2 bits to hear the staircase.

blocks.caption: With Fₛ = 1000 Hz: every frequency above 500 folds back onto its mirror image below 500 (F₂ = Fₛ − F₁, the Lab 2 Q15 pattern). 900 Hz is indistinguishable from 100 Hz after sampling. Hover any part.

blocks.body: Lab 2 Q14 vs Q15: the **Nyquist frequency** is Fₛ/2. **Fₛ − F** is the *alias* of F (that's Q15). Q14 puts Fₛ − F in the choices to catch you.

blocks.prompt: A 7 kHz tone is sampled at 10 kHz. What frequency does it show up as?
blocks.answer: Nyquist is 5 kHz, 7 is above it, so it folds: 10 − 7 = 3 kHz.

blocks.prompt: Why do phone calls sound dull?
blocks.answer: Phones sample at 8,000 Hz, so Nyquist is 4,000 Hz. Everything above 4 kHz (the crisp s and f sounds) is filtered out before sampling.

blocks.title: Why the rule works (optional, for the curious)
blocks.body:
Samples are taken at t = n/Fₛ. Compare cos(2π·F·t) and cos(2π·(F + Fₛ)·t) at those moments:

  cos(2π·(F + Fₛ)·n/Fₛ) = cos(2π·F·n/Fₛ + 2π·n)

2π·n is n whole laps of the circle, which changes nothing.
So both waves give identical samples. The same trick with cos(−θ) = cos(θ) gives the mirror Fₛ − F.

exercises.title: Samples, spacing, and x[n]
exercises.prompt: x(t) = cos(2π·50·t) is sampled at Fₛ = 400 Hz for 0.1 s. (a) What is Tₛ? (b) How many samples? (c) Write x[n]. (d) How many samples per repeat of the wave?
hints: samples = seconds × Fₛ. For x[n], replace t with n/Fₛ.
One repeat lasts 1/50 s. How many samples fit in that?
exercises.why: Every speech tool you'll use (Praat, librosa, Whisper) starts by doing exactly this.

exercises.title: Find the alias
exercises.prompt: A phone line samples at Fₛ = 8,000 Hz. (a) Nyquist? (b) A 5,000 Hz whistle gets in. What does it show up as? (c) A 9,000 Hz tone?
hints: 5,000 is between Nyquist and Fₛ: mirror it, Fₛ − F.
9,000 is above Fₛ: subtract Fₛ first.
exercises.why: This is why every microphone chip has a filter that removes high frequencies BEFORE sampling: once aliasing happens, no software can undo it.

choices.feedback: Right: Nyquist is 4,000; 6,000 is above it, so it folds to 8,000 − 6,000 = 2,000.

4,000 is the Nyquist frequency itself, not the alias.

exercises.title: Better copy
exercises.prompt: Which change gives a more accurate copy of the wave? (Lab 2 Q9)
hints: Read each option out loud and cross off the ones that are clearly wrong.
The chapter's cards in this section have the exact fact you need.
Pick the one that matches the definition word for word.
solution: Higher Fₛ (equivalently, shorter Tₛ) = more points per cycle.
exercises.why: The sample-rate menu in every audio app is this choice.

choices.feedback: Right: more samples per second trace the wave more closely.
Longer just gives more samples of the same quality.
Fewer samples per second = worse copy (and more aliasing).
You're measuring the wave; you don't get to change it.
